screens.title: Arrays and ArrayLists: fixed rows and flexible lists
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore two foundational collection types in Java: arrays and ArrayList. Arrays give you a fixed-size, contiguous block of storage with very fast index access. You use them when the number of elements is known and stable. ArrayList provides a resizable list built on top of an array that grows and shrinks for you, which is ideal when the collection size can change at runtime. You will see how to declare and initialize arrays, how to access and update elements, and why accessing an invalid index causes a runtime exception. Then we'll look at ArrayList operations: adding, getting, setting, removing, and checking size. We'll also address generics, autoboxing, and common beginner mistakes like forgetting to initialize a list or modifying a list while iterating. By the end of this chapter you will know when a raw array is a good choice and when ArrayList reduces boilerplate and runtime copying. Consider a classroom of student scores: if class size is fixed for a test, an array is fine; if students join or leave, ArrayList saves you repeated manual copying. Which pattern will fit your next program?

Arrays and ArrayLists

Fixed-size arrays give direct index access. ArrayList gives automatic resizing and convenient methods for common operations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will be able to explain what an array is: a fixed-size container that stores elements of one type and provides direct, index-based access. You will practice writing declarations and initializing arrays with known sizes or inline values. Second, you will confidently use array indexing to read and update elements and recognize the bounds rule that valid indices run from zero to length minus one. Third, you will understand ArrayList as a resizable list implementation: how to create one, add and retrieve elements, and why its internal array may be replaced during growth. Finally, you will implement common ArrayList operations such as add, get, set, remove, and size, and reason about autoboxing when storing primitives. Each objective ties a practical coding skill to why it matters: correctness, flexibility, and avoiding common runtime exceptions. These skills let you pick the right structure for collections in everyday Java programs and avoid beginner pitfalls like null references or index errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — practice and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on applying features and avoiding common pitfalls. First, practice safe indexing and learn how to read the array length so you never attempt an out-of-bounds access. A practical habit is to use loop conditions tied to length or size rather than hard-coded indices. Second, practice initializing collections before calling methods; an uninitialized ArrayList reference will cause a null pointer problem when you try to add elements. Third, practice safe modification patterns—if you remove elements while iterating with a basic for loop, indices shift and you may skip or mis-handle elements. Learn to remove using iterators when you need to change a list while looping. Fourth, practice choosing the right structure: arrays when size is stable and performance-critical, ArrayList when flexibility and simpler code are more important. Each objective pairs a small habit with the reason it reduces bugs and simplifies maintenance, helping you write code that behaves predictably in real applications.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Practice & Pitfalls
Safe indexing
  • Always use array length or list size in loop conditions.
  • Remember indices start at zero; last index is length minus one.
  • Accessing an invalid index causes a runtime ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Initialization
Create your ArrayList with a constructor before calling methods to avoid null pointer errors.
Safe modification
If you must remove while iterating, prefer an iterator to avoid skipping elements due to shifting indices.
Quick habit checklist
Check bounds
Use length or size rather than constants inside loops.
Init lists
Always call the constructor before add or get operations.
Safe remove
Use iterators during removal to maintain consistent behavior.

screens.title: What is a Java array?
screens.narratorSegment: An array in Java is a container object that holds a fixed number of values of a single type. Think of it as a row of identical mailboxes: each mailbox holds one value and has a number, starting at zero. This numbering is called zero-based indexing. The key properties are fixed length and homogeneous type. Fixed length means once you create an array with a given size, that number of slots does not change. Homogeneous type means every slot holds the same declared type, for example integers or strings. This structure gives very fast direct access: retrieving or writing an element by index is an O(1) operation because the runtime computes the memory location directly. A concrete example is storing ten test scores when you know there are exactly ten students; an array of size ten models that perfectly. A common misconception is thinking arrays can grow automatically — they cannot. Trying to access or assign outside the valid index range causes a runtime ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. To avoid that, always check the array length or use loops that iterate from zero up to length minus one. Key takeaway: arrays are simple, efficient, and predictable when size and element type are fixed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is an array?
Core definition

An array stores a fixed number of values of the same type and provides direct access by index beginning at zero.

Key properties
  • Fixed size: create with a specified length and it does not change.
  • Typed: every element matches the declared element type.
  • Indexing: elements accessed with indices 0 through length minus one.
  • Fast access: direct index lookup is constant time.
Analogy: mailboxes
Each mailbox is a slot with a number; you address the slot by that number.
Common misconception
Arrays do not resize automatically; you must create a new array and copy elements to grow capacity.
Concrete example
int[] scores = new int[10]; scores[0] = 85; int first = scores[0];
Check your understanding
If you have an array of size N, valid indices are 0 through N minus 1. Trying to access index N causes a runtime error.
Key Takeaway

Arrays are efficient and simple, and ideal when the collection size is known and stable.

screens.title: Declaring, initializing, and accessing arrays
screens.narratorSegment: Declaring and initializing arrays is a two-step idea: first you state the element type and name, then you allocate the slots. In code you declare a reference that will point to an array, then use a constructor-like allocation to set the size. You can also declare and initialize inline with explicit values. When you access elements, you use the index to read or assign a value. A concrete example is a scores array for ten students. When you write code, favor loops that reference the array length property instead of hard-coded bounds. This avoids off-by-one errors. A common beginner mistake is misunderstanding when an array reference has not been initialized. Declaring the reference without allocating the array leads to a null reference; attempting to read or write then causes a null pointer problem. Another issue arises when swapping between declarations that initialize inline and those that allocate size first: be explicit and consistent. Practice by writing small loops that set or print every element, using length in the loop condition. That habit removes most indexing bugs and improves code clarity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Declaring & Accessing
Common patterns
Declare a reference, then allocate with a size, or declare and initialize in one step. Use length when iterating.
// declaration then allocation int[] scores; scores = new int[10]; // declare and initialize inline int[] scores2 = {85, 92, 78, 95, 88}; // access and update int first = scores2[0]; scores2[2] = 80;
Explanation bullets
  • Declaration names the type of elements and the variable that will refer to the array.
  • Allocation with a size reserves fixed slots; inline initialization sets values immediately.
  • Access uses 0-based index; updating uses assignment with an index.
Concrete scenario
Imagine you receive a class roster with known size for a test. Create an array with that size, fill each slot as you read student scores, and later compute the average by iterating up to length.
Common mistake

Using a literal index that exceeds length causes a runtime error. Rely on length in loops to prevent that.

Try this
Write a loop that prints each element using i from zero up to array length minus one. Verify you never attempt index equal to length.

screens.title: Why arrays are limited — and how resizing works manually
screens.narratorSegment: The main limitation of arrays is their fixed size. If you need a larger collection, you must create a new, larger array and copy existing elements into it. This manual resizing is a multi-step process: allocate a new array with the desired larger size, iterate over the old array to copy each element into the new array, then let the old array be discarded so the runtime can reclaim its memory. That copying step has a cost proportional to the number of elements copied, so frequent resizing by one element at a time is inefficient. A concrete scenario: if you begin with an array of size five and need to add a sixth element, you would create a new array size six or larger, copy five values, then place the new value. This pattern explains why many dynamic collections adopt growth strategies—allocating extra capacity and growing by a factor to amortize copies. The takeaway is: arrays are inexpensive when size is known and stable, but manual resizing introduces time and code complexity. When you need many dynamic changes, a resizable abstraction is preferable.

keyIdea.title: Resizing cost
keyIdea.text: Growing a raw array requires allocating new memory and copying elements, which can be costly when done frequently.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Manual Resizing
Resizing steps
  1. Create a new larger array.
  2. Copy each element from the old array into the new one.
  3. Replace the reference so the program uses the new array.
  4. Allow the old array to be reclaimed by the runtime.
Performance note
Copying is linear in the number of elements. If resizing happens often, the total cost grows. Amortized growth strategies reduce average cost per insertion.
Concrete analogy
Think of moving mail from a short row of mailboxes into a longer row: you must move each letter by hand. Doing that for many new letters is tedious, which is why automatic resizing strategies add extra capacity at once.
Why it matters

Frequent manual copying is a hidden cost; prefer a dynamic list when many inserts are expected.

screens.title: ArrayList internals and automatic resizing
screens.narratorSegment: ArrayList is a resizable list implementation from Java's Collections Framework that gives you a familiar list A P I while handling resizing internally. Internally, ArrayList maintains a regular array. When you add elements and the internal array becomes full, ArrayList creates a new internal array, typically larger than the previous one, copies existing elements into it, and then continues. This growth strategy avoids copying on every single addition by increasing capacity by a factor, amortizing the cost of copy operations over many additions. From a programmer's view you call add to append an element, get to read by index, set to replace an element at a given index, remove to delete, and size to check the current element count. One important detail is that ArrayList stores objects, not primitives. That is why we use wrapper types like Integer for numeric collections and rely on autoboxing and unboxing to convert between primitives and wrappers. A common pitfall is forgetting to initialize the ArrayList reference before use, which leads to a null pointer problem. ArrayList simplifies code compared to manual resizing and is the usual choice when collection size changes are common.

keyIdea.title: ArrayList essence
keyIdea.text: ArrayList wraps an internal array and resizes it automatically, offering a convenient API with amortized growth behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › ArrayList Internals
How it works
  • ArrayList holds an internal array of objects.
  • When full, it creates a larger array and copies existing elements.
  • Growth is usually by a factor to reduce frequent copying.
Common API
  • add(element): append an element.
  • get(index): retrieve an element by index.
  • set(index, element): replace an element.
  • remove(index or object): delete an element.
  • size(): current number of elements.
Concrete example
Create a list of student names using generics for type safety. When you add more names than the current capacity, ArrayList transparently resizes so you can focus on application logic instead of array bookkeeping.
Note on primitives
ArrayList stores objects. Use wrapper types like Integer for numbers; autoboxing converts primitives automatically when you add or retrieve values.
Key Takeaway

ArrayList offers convenience and amortized performance by hiding resizing logic behind a simple API.

screens.title: Common ArrayList operations with code examples
screens.narratorSegment: Working with ArrayList is primarily about a few simple methods. To add an element, call add; to read by position, call get; to replace an element, call set; to delete, call remove; and to learn how many elements are stored, call size. These operations produce intuitive behavior: add increases size, get retrieves the element at the given index, set returns the previous value at an index while replacing it, and remove shrinks the list and shifts subsequent elements left. A concrete code walkthrough grounds these ideas: create an empty list of names, add a handful of student names, read the first name, update the first name, and remove another student. Keep in mind bounds rules: get and set require a valid index less than size. Also remember that remove by object deletes the first matching element and remove by index deletes at that position. When storing primitive values, store wrapper types and rely on autoboxing. Practicing these methods with small lists reveals how indices shift after removals and why verifying size before accessing indices is a good habit. Common ArrayList operations with code examples means master add, get, set, remove, and size; watch index bounds and index shifts after removals.. In practical terms, add, get, set, remove, and size in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Master add, get, set, remove, and size; watch index bounds and index shifts after removals.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › ArrayList Operations
Example code
import java.util.ArrayList; ArrayList<String> studentNames = new ArrayList<>(); studentNames.add("Alice"); studentNames.add("Bob"); String first = studentNames.get(0); // "Alice" studentNames.set(0, "Alicia"); // replaces "Alice" studentNames.remove("Bob"); int count = studentNames.size();
This snippet shows typical calls. Remember get and set need an index within current size; remove by object removes the first match and shifts later elements.
Explanation bullets
  • add appends and increments size.
  • get reads without changing size; set replaces a value at an index.
  • remove can remove by index or by object; indices shift left after removal.
  • size reports the current number of stored elements, not capacity.
Key Takeaway

Use size checks before get or set, and be mindful that remove changes subsequent indices.

screens.title: Generics, autoboxing, and primitive types
screens.narratorSegment: ArrayList works with objects, not primitive types. Generics allow you to specify the element type for compile-time safety, for example indicating that a list will only contain strings. When you need to store numeric primitives like int, use the corresponding wrapper class such as Integer. Java provides autoboxing and unboxing so that primitive literals convert automatically when added to a list and convert back when retrieved. For example, adding the number twenty five to a list of Integer will autobox the primitive into an Integer object; retrieving it and assigning to an int variable will unbox it automatically. This feature makes using lists convenient, but it's important to remember the memory and performance implications: wrappers are objects and involve additional overhead compared to raw primitives. A common beginner error is to assume ArrayList can hold primitives directly; compilation prevents that and forces you to use the wrapper type. Generics also give compile-time type checks, reducing casting errors. Key takeaway: use generics for type safety and rely on autoboxing to bridge primitives and objects, while being aware of wrapper overhead. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Generics & Autoboxing
Generics
Specify the element type when declaring an ArrayList to get compile-time checks and avoid casting at runtime.
Example
ArrayList of String ensures only strings are added; compiler will flag attempts to add a different type.
Autoboxing and wrappers
ArrayList cannot store primitive types. Use Integer, Double, Boolean, etc., and Java will autobox and unbox between primitives and wrappers automatically.
Practical note
Wrappers are objects and carry overhead. For tight performance or memory needs, primitive arrays remain more efficient.

screens.title: When to choose array vs ArrayList
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an array and an ArrayList depends on your needs for fixed size, performance, and convenience. Use an array when the number of elements is known ahead of time and unlikely to change, or when you want the lowest overhead for primitive storage. Arrays offer slightly better raw performance and memory usage because they store primitives directly and have minimal metadata. Use ArrayList when you need a flexible collection that can grow and shrink without manual copying, and when the convenience of methods like add, remove, and size reduces code complexity. ArrayList is the pragmatic choice for most application-level code because it hides resizing and provides type-safe generics. Watch for common pitfalls: arrays throw index errors when you go out of bounds; ArrayList can throw a runtime error if you forget to initialize it. Also remember that removing elements shifts indices, which affects loops that depend on stable indexing. The practical rule: prefer ArrayList for general collections and arrays for fixed-size, performance-sensitive contexts. In practical terms, trade-offs: performance, flexibility, and simplicity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Arrays

screens.title: Student Grade Manager — a hands-on example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work through a practical example used in this chapter: a student grade manager implemented with two ArrayList instances, one for names and one for grades. This pattern pairs parallel lists to represent related data and keeps indices aligned so a name at position i corresponds to the grade at position i. The steps are straightforward: create both lists, add at least five names and grades, print the roster by iterating using size, update a given student's grade by finding the index using an index-of operation and then calling set, remove a student by finding their index and removing from both lists, and finally print the updated roster. This concrete workflow highlights several important ideas: verifying that indexOf returns a valid index before using it, keeping the parallel arrays in sync when removing, and using size in loops to avoid out-of-bounds access. A common pitfall is forgetting to remove the grade when removing the name, which leaves lists out of sync. Starter code
import java.util.ArrayList; public class StudentGradeManager { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList<String> studentNames = new ArrayList<>(); ArrayList<Integer> studentGrades = new ArrayList<>(); // add five students and grades studentNames.add("Alice"); studentGrades.add(85); studentNames.add("Bob"); studentGrades.add(92); studentNames.add("Charlie"); studentGrades.add(78); studentNames.add("David"); studentGrades.add(95); studentNames.add("Eve"); studentGrades.add(88); } }
Implementation pointers
  • Print the roster by looping from zero to size minus one and calling get for each list.
  • Update a grade by finding the student's index with indexOf, then set on the grades list when index is valid.
  • Remove a student by removing from both lists at the same index to keep alignment.

Parallel lists are simple but require careful index management. For more complex data, consider a single list of objects pairing name and grade.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore two foundational collection types in Java: arrays and ArrayList. Arrays give you a fixed-size, contiguous block of storage with very fast index access. You use them when the number of elements is known and stable. ArrayList provides a resizable list built on top of an array that grows and shrinks for you, which is ideal when the collection size can change at runtime. You will see how to declare and initialize arrays, how to access and update elements, and why accessing an invalid index causes a runtime exception. Then we'll look at ArrayList operations: adding, getting, setting, removing, and checking size. We'll also address generics, autoboxing, and common beginner mistakes like forgetting to initialize a list or modifying a list while iterating. By the end of this chapter you will know when a raw array is a good choice and when ArrayList reduces boilerplate and runtime copying. Consider a classroom of student scores: if class size is fixed for a test, an array is fine; if students join or leave, ArrayList saves you repeated manual copying. Which pattern will fit your next program?

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will be able to explain what an array is: a fixed-size container that stores elements of one type and provides direct, index-based access. You will practice writing declarations and initializing arrays with known sizes or inline values. Second, you will confidently use array indexing to read and update elements and recognize the bounds rule that valid indices run from zero to length minus one. Third, you will understand ArrayList as a resizable list implementation: how to create one, add and retrieve elements, and why its internal array may be replaced during growth. Finally, you will implement common ArrayList operations such as add, get, set, remove, and size, and reason about autoboxing when storing primitives. Each objective ties a practical coding skill to why it matters: correctness, flexibility, and avoiding common runtime exceptions. These skills let you pick the right structure for collections in everyday Java programs and avoid beginner pitfalls like null references or index errors.

These objectives focus on applying features and avoiding common pitfalls. First, practice safe indexing and learn how to read the array length so you never attempt an out-of-bounds access. A practical habit is to use loop conditions tied to length or size rather than hard-coded indices. Second, practice initializing collections before calling methods; an uninitialized ArrayList reference will cause a null pointer problem when you try to add elements. Third, practice safe modification patterns—if you remove elements while iterating with a basic for loop, indices shift and you may skip or mis-handle elements. Learn to remove using iterators when you need to change a list while looping. Fourth, practice choosing the right structure: arrays when size is stable and performance-critical, ArrayList when flexibility and simpler code are more important. Each objective pairs a small habit with the reason it reduces bugs and simplifies maintenance, helping you write code that behaves predictably in real applications.

An array in Java is a container object that holds a fixed number of values of a single type. Think of it as a row of identical mailboxes: each mailbox holds one value and has a number, starting at zero. This numbering is called zero-based indexing. The key properties are fixed length and homogeneous type. Fixed length means once you create an array with a given size, that number of slots does not change. Homogeneous type means every slot holds the same declared type, for example integers or strings. This structure gives very fast direct access: retrieving or writing an element by index is an O(1) operation because the runtime computes the memory location directly. A concrete example is storing ten test scores when you know there are exactly ten students; an array of size ten models that perfectly. A common misconception is thinking arrays can grow automatically — they cannot. Trying to access or assign outside the valid index range causes a runtime ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. To avoid that, always check the array length or use loops that iterate from zero up to length minus one. Key takeaway: arrays are simple, efficient, and predictable when size and element type are fixed.

Declaring and initializing arrays is a two-step idea: first you state the element type and name, then you allocate the slots. In code you declare a reference that will point to an array, then use a constructor-like allocation to set the size. You can also declare and initialize inline with explicit values. When you access elements, you use the index to read or assign a value. A concrete example is a scores array for ten students. When you write code, favor loops that reference the array length property instead of hard-coded bounds. This avoids off-by-one errors. A common beginner mistake is misunderstanding when an array reference has not been initialized. Declaring the reference without allocating the array leads to a null reference; attempting to read or write then causes a null pointer problem. Another issue arises when swapping between declarations that initialize inline and those that allocate size first: be explicit and consistent. Practice by writing small loops that set or print every element, using length in the loop condition. That habit removes most indexing bugs and improves code clarity.

The main limitation of arrays is their fixed size. If you need a larger collection, you must create a new, larger array and copy existing elements into it. This manual resizing is a multi-step process: allocate a new array with the desired larger size, iterate over the old array to copy each element into the new array, then let the old array be discarded so the runtime can reclaim its memory. That copying step has a cost proportional to the number of elements copied, so frequent resizing by one element at a time is inefficient. A concrete scenario: if you begin with an array of size five and need to add a sixth element, you would create a new array size six or larger, copy five values, then place the new value. This pattern explains why many dynamic collections adopt growth strategies—allocating extra capacity and growing by a factor to amortize copies. The takeaway is: arrays are inexpensive when size is known and stable, but manual resizing introduces time and code complexity. When you need many dynamic changes, a resizable abstraction is preferable.

ArrayList is a resizable list implementation from Java's Collections Framework that gives you a familiar list A P I while handling resizing internally. Internally, ArrayList maintains a regular array. When you add elements and the internal array becomes full, ArrayList creates a new internal array, typically larger than the previous one, copies existing elements into it, and then continues. This growth strategy avoids copying on every single addition by increasing capacity by a factor, amortizing the cost of copy operations over many additions. From a programmer's view you call add to append an element, get to read by index, set to replace an element at a given index, remove to delete, and size to check the current element count. One important detail is that ArrayList stores objects, not primitives. That is why we use wrapper types like Integer for numeric collections and rely on autoboxing and unboxing to convert between primitives and wrappers. A common pitfall is forgetting to initialize the ArrayList reference before use, which leads to a null pointer problem. ArrayList simplifies code compared to manual resizing and is the usual choice when collection size changes are common.

Working with ArrayList is primarily about a few simple methods. To add an element, call add; to read by position, call get; to replace an element, call set; to delete, call remove; and to learn how many elements are stored, call size. These operations produce intuitive behavior: add increases size, get retrieves the element at the given index, set returns the previous value at an index while replacing it, and remove shrinks the list and shifts subsequent elements left. A concrete code walkthrough grounds these ideas: create an empty list of names, add a handful of student names, read the first name, update the first name, and remove another student. Keep in mind bounds rules: get and set require a valid index less than size. Also remember that remove by object deletes the first matching element and remove by index deletes at that position. When storing primitive values, store wrapper types and rely on autoboxing. Practicing these methods with small lists reveals how indices shift after removals and why verifying size before accessing indices is a good habit. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ArrayList works with objects, not primitive types. Generics allow you to specify the element type for compile-time safety, for example indicating that a list will only contain strings. When you need to store numeric primitives like int, use the corresponding wrapper class such as Integer. Java provides autoboxing and unboxing so that primitive literals convert automatically when added to a list and convert back when retrieved. For example, adding the number twenty five to a list of Integer will autobox the primitive into an Integer object; retrieving it and assigning to an int variable will unbox it automatically. This feature makes using lists convenient, but it's important to remember the memory and performance implications: wrappers are objects and involve additional overhead compared to raw primitives. A common beginner error is to assume ArrayList can hold primitives directly; compilation prevents that and forces you to use the wrapper type. Generics also give compile-time type checks, reducing casting errors. Key takeaway: use generics for type safety and rely on autoboxing to bridge primitives and objects, while being aware of wrapper overhead. Choosing between an array and an ArrayList depends on your needs for fixed size, performance, and convenience. Use an array when the number of elements is known ahead of time and unlikely to change, or when you want the lowest overhead for primitive storage. Arrays offer slightly better raw performance and memory usage because they store primitives directly and have minimal metadata. Use ArrayList when you need a flexible collection that can grow and shrink without manual copying, and when the convenience of methods like add, remove, and size reduces code complexity. ArrayList is the pragmatic choice for most application-level code because it hides resizing and provides type-safe generics.
